answer:
According to the clinical guidelines reviewed, high-intensity statin therapy should be recommended for patients with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and for primary prevention in adults aged 40-75 years old with LDL-C levels ≥190 mg/dL or those with diabetes mellitus who have additional risk factors. These recommendations are found in the ACC/AHA Multi-Society Cholesterol Guideline from 2018 [ACC/AHA, 2018]. No other specific population criteria for high-intensity statin therapy in primary prevention were provided by these guidelines.

The ACC/AHA Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease Guideline does not explicitly mention a similar intensity recommendation for primary prevention using aspirin; there is no routine recommendation for aspirin for primary prevention, except under certain conditions specified by the clinician. [ACC/AHA, 2019]. 

Given the information available from these guidelines, patients who qualify based on clinical criteria (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or specific patient characteristics such as high LDL-C levels and diabetes) and without other risk factors would be candidates for receiving high-intensity statin therapy in primary prevention. For aspirin usage, further risk-benefit discussions with clinicians are advised outside of the standard guidelines described.

results.content: High-intensity statin therapy is recommended for patients with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and for primary prevention in adults 40-75 years with LDL-C >=190 mg/dL or diabetes with additional risk factors.

Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease is not routinely recommended due to bleeding risk, except in select high-risk adults 40-70 years after a risk-benefit discussion with their clinician.
